items.summary: Standalone streamable-http mode in datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server rejects forged Host and Origin headers on /mcp, but custom management routes mounted on the same application do not get the same browser-origin protection. A malicious website can keep an attacker origin while its hostname resolves to 127.0.0.1 or a private target address, then send PUT /api/connect to replace the MCP server's active Jupyter backend. The route accepts the browser-shaped request and makes the server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure.The protected /mcp endpoint shows the intended browser-origin boundary. With MCP_TOKEN configured, /mcp rejects forged browser headers:POST /mcp with Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKENHost: attacker.example:8142Origin: http://attacker.example:8142HTTP 421 Invalid Host headerThe vulnerable route is jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187. It parses caller JSON, updates the active Jupyter backend configuration, resets ServerContext, and starts the kernel without applying the /mcp Host/Origin rejection to the custom items.title: [flyto-core] Flyto2 Core: SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding (validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning)
items.summary: [MEDIUM] SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding — validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinningCWE: CWE-918 (SSRF) / CWE-367 (TOCTOU).CVSS v3.1: AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N = 6.8 Medium (AC:H — needs attacker-controlled DNS with a low/zero TTL and to flip the answer between the guard's lookup and the connection's lookup; S:C — reaches internal/metadata services the guard is meant to block; C:H — e.g. cloud metadata credentials at 169.254.169.254).Affected component: flyto-core (PyPI flyto-core), HEAD ae2b38e (v2.26.7). src/core/utils.py::validate_url_ssrf (resolution at getaddrinfo ~L512, is_private_ip check ~L515) and every consumer: guarded_aiohttp_request(), enforce_outbound_url()/validate_url_with_env_config() — i.e. http.get/request/batch, graphql.query/mutation, monitor.http_check, notification.{slack,discord,teams}, ai.vision_analyze, verify.visual_diff, browser.proxy_rotate, etc.Relationship: Incomplete hardening of the SSRF-guard family (GHSA-pgwh-4jj4-qm8v, GHSA-c9hr-64h3-gxpc, GHSA-794r-5rp2-fpg8/CVE-2026-55787). Those fixes added per-module coverage, redirect revalidation, and IPv6-transition range-checks — but none pins the resolved address, so the guard's resolve-then-connect gap defeats all of them.Root causevalidate_url_ssrf() resolves the hostname with socket.getaddrinfo() and rejects the URL if any resolved IP is private. It then returns the URL string (hostname intact). The caller (guarded_aiohttp_request: validate_url_with_env_config(url) then session.request(method, url, ...)) hands the hostname to aiohttp, which performs an independent second DNS resolution at connect time. The validated IP is never pinned for the connection, so an attacker whose authoritative DNS returns a public A record for the guard's lookup and a private/loopback/metadata address for the connection's lookup reaches internal space. aiohttp resolves via its own resolver, distinct from the guard's socket.getaddrinfo, so the two lookups are genuinely separate — one flip is sufficient.ReachabilityAttacker controls DNS for rebind.attacker.test (TTL 0), and drives any guarded HTTP module with url=http://rebind.attacker.test/ (recipe / MCP execute_module).Guard: getaddrinfo → public IP → is_private_ip false → URL allowed.Outbound request: aiohttp re-resolves rebind.attacker.test → attacker now answers 127.0.0.1 / 169.254.169.254 → connects to the internal target. Redirect revalidation (GHSA-c9hr) does not help — the initial hop already rebinds.Executable PoC (benign, local; deterministic)The attacker's TTL=0 flip is modelled by making socket.getaddrinfo return public on lookup #1 (the guard's) and loopback on later lookups (the connection's); a raw local TCP sentinel stands in for the internal service. No payload is sent.# (full source: findings/flyto-core/raw/poc_dns_rebinding.py)# guard sees resolution #1 (public) -> ALLOWS;  connect re-resolves (127.0.0.1) -> hits sentinelvalidate_url_ssrf("http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/")     # ALLOWEDsocket.create_connection(("rebind.attacker.test", 8080))   # lands on 127.0.0.1 sentinelObserved output:[guard] validate_url_ssrf ALLOWED http://rebind.attacker.test:8080/  (saw public 93.184.216.34 on resolution #1)[connect] outbound request re-resolved rebind.attacker.test -> 127.0.0.1 and reached the INTERNAL sentinel: TrueBUG CONFIRMED: guard passed but connection reached the private/internal IP (DNS rebinding, no IP pin)Adversarial re-readIs the getaddrinfo monkeypatch cheating? No — it deterministically models an attacker's TTL=0 authoritative DNS returning different answers to two separate lookups. The code gap is real and unavoidable: validate_url_with_env_config(url) resolves once, then session.request(url) resolves again with no pin.Does aiohttp's DNS cache prevent it? No — the guard's socket.getaddrinfo and aiohttp's resolver are independent; aiohttp caches its OWN (malicious) lookup, not the guard's.Does redirect revalidation (GHSA-c9hr) block it? No — the first hop rebinds before any redirect.Multiple A records? The guard loops all getaddrinfo results and rejects if any is private, so static multi-record does not bypass; only a time-of-use flip does.Result: no concrete blocker. CONFIRMED (Medium; AC:H because it needs attacker DNS + a flip).RemediationPin the validated address: resolve once, validate every returned IP, then connect to the pinned IP (not the hostname) — e.g. pass the resolved address to aiohttp via a custom resolver/TCPConnector (or set the Host header and connect by IP), so the guard's decision and the socket target are the same address. Apply for every hop in guarded_aiohttp_request. Alternatively, use a resolver wrapper that validates inside the connect path.ConfidenceHigh that the resolve-then-connect gap exists and the guard is bypassable by rebinding (PoC fires against the real guard). Severity Medium due to the AC:H rebinding precondition.Proof-of-Concept source (poc_dns_rebinding.py)"""PoC: DNS-rebinding SSRF bypass of validate_url_

items.title: [flyto-core] Flyto2 Core: http.paginate follows server-supplied next-page URLs (Link header / cursor) without SSRF revalidation
items.summary: Summaryhttp.paginate validates only the initial base_url, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 Link: rel="next" headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop without revalidating each follow-up URL. An attacker's first-page response can point next at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.Root Causesrc/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495 validates base_url (first URL only). The pagination loop _paginate_link_header reads next_url via _parse_link_header (:203), sets url=next_url (:208), and calls session.request(method, url) (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).ImpactReadable second-order SSRF that bypasses the SSRF control; internal/metadata body aggregated into all_items and returned to the caller (C:H, S:C).Proof of ConceptVerified live: http.paginate with allowlisted base 127.0.0.1 followed a Link: <http://127.0.0.3/...>; rel="next" (non-allowlisted) and returned INTERNAL-NEXTPAGE-SECRET in the aggregated items.execute_module http.paginate {"url":"http://attacker.tld/p1","strategy":"link_header"}attacker p1 response header: Link: <http://<cloud-metadata-ip>/latest/meta-data/>; rel="next"Attack ChainEntry: http.paginate {url:"http://attacker.tld/p1", strategy:"link_header"}. Guard: validate_url_with_env_config(base_url) (paginate.py:495) — validates the FIRST url only.Sink: _paginate_link_header reads next_url (_parse_link_header :203), url=next_url (:208), session.request(method,url) (:196) — NO validate call in the loop. Bypass proof: only :495 validates; loop at :186-208 has zero guard calls.Impact: internal body aggregated into all_items and returned → readable second-order SSRF.Bypass EvidenceLive PoC followed a Link header into non-allowlisted loopback and returned the internal marker in aggregated results. Only base_url is validated; the follow loop never revalidates.Affected Versions<= 2.26.6 — paginate.py:495 + loop present on latest release tag.Suggested FixRun every follow-up URL (Link header, cursor, offset target) through validate_url_with_env_config before fetching it inside the pagination loop.CreditVulnerability discovered by zx (Jace).Referenceshttps://github.com/flytohub/flyto-core/security/advisories/GHSA-2mr3-rxrq-238chttps://github.com/flytohub/flyto-core/commit/bbb6f1cfec22fee1ea0e6ecf1129d7103c85e09fhttps://github.com/flytohub/flyto-core/releases/tag/v2.26.8https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2mr3-rxrq-238c

items.title: [flyto-core] Flyto2 Core: SSRF guard validates the resolved IP but connects by hostname, allowing DNS-rebinding TOCTOU
items.summary: Summaryvalidate_url_ssrf resolves the hostname, checks the IP against private ranges, then discards the IP and returns the hostname URL string. aiohttp performs a fresh, independent DNS resolution at connect time. An attacker controlling DNS for a hostname (TTL 0, alternating public IP and internal IP) passes validation on the first lookup and connects to the internal IP on the second — a classic check-then-use race. SECURITY_SSRF.md line 63 explicitly claims DNS-rebinding is prevented; it is not.Root Causesrc/core/utils.py:523 returns the hostname URL after validation; the resolved IP is never pinned. A repo grep of http/ and utils.py for TCPConnector / resolver / response.history / on_request_redirect / IP-pinning returns NONE. Each module builds a fresh ClientSession per call → the connect-time getaddrinfo is independent of the validation-time lookup.ImpactDefeats the SSRF guard on ALL modules that call it (readable internal fetch). Independent of IP-range completeness — the private IP is never presented to is_private_ip. Requires attacker DNS control + winning the resolution race → AC:H.Proof of ConceptCode-proven: validate_url_ssrf returns the hostname (utils.py:523); no pinned-IP connector anywhere. Two independent resolutions occur (validation-time and aiohttp connect-time).attacker DNS: rebind.attacker.tld TTL 0, alternating public IP and the cloud metadata IPexecute_module http.get {"url":"http://rebind.attacker.tld/latest/meta-data/..."}Attack ChainEntry: http.get {url:"http://rebind.attacker.tld/..."}. Guard: validate_url_with_env_config. Bypass proof: getaddrinfo(rebind.attacker.tld) returns the public IP, is_private_ip=False (utils.py:511-519); returns the hostname URL (:523) — the IP is discarded.Sink: session.get("http://rebind.attacker.tld/...") (get.py:116). aiohttp performs a FRESH independent getaddrinfo at connect → now resolves to the internal IP. Bypass proof: no TCPConnector/AsyncResolver/pinned-IP in http/ (grep confirms none). Two lookups.Impact: internal fetch, body returned.Bypass Evidenceutils.py:523 returns the hostname string, not a pinned IP; grep confirms no IP pinning or custom resolver anywhere on the path; fresh ClientSession per call guarantees an independent second resolution.Affected Versions<= 2.26.6 — utils.py:523 present on latest release tag; no pinning added on HEAD.Suggested FixResolve the hostname once, pin the validated IP, and connect to that IP (custom TCPConnector/resolver) — reject any connect-time resolution that differs. This is the fix SECURITY_SSRF.md already claims is in place.CreditVulnerability discovered by zx (Jace).Referenceshttps://github.com/flytohub/flyto-core/security/advisories/GHSA-pfg2-w999-497vhttps://github.com/flytohub/flyto-core/commit/bf748df864d348004cf45d830bc59f62c5c4a58ahttps://github.com/flytohub/flyto-core/releases/tag/v2.26.8https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfg2-w999-497v

items.title: [flyto-core] Flyto2 Core: Arbitrary file write via unguarded data.*/file.* modules (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-67429)
items.summary: [CRITICAL] Arbitrary file write via unguarded data.* / file.* write modules — incomplete fix of GHSA-2956CWE: CWE-22 (Path Traversal) / CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path); impact reaches CWE-94 (code execution via file overwrite).CVSS v3.1: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.3 Critical (S:C because a write escapes the intended sandbox confinement into the host filesystem / other components).AV:N — reachable via the MCP server / recipe engine (execute_module). AC:L — deterministic. PR:L — any client able to run a module/recipe (the same attacker model as GHSA-2956; unauthenticated on the HTTP MCP surface per CVE-2026-55786). UI:N. S:C — escapes FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR. C/I/A:H — arbitrary-content write to any absolute path → overwrite app code / recipes / ~/.bashrc / cron / authorized_keys → RCE.Affected component: flyto-core (PyPI flyto-core), HEAD ae2b38e (v2.26.7 line). Modules data.csv.write (src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py), data.json_to_csv (.../data/json_to_csv.py), file.copy (.../file/copy.py), file.move (.../file/move.py) — and the broader data.*/file.*/report-writer families that do not call the path guard.Relationship: Incomplete fix of GHSA-2956-977x-2w3r (Critical arbitrary file write, patched in v2.26.6 by commit d5f89d7). That fix routed a hand-picked module list (image.download/convert/resize/crop/compress/rotate/watermark/qrcode_generate, document.excel_write/pdf_fill_form/word_to_pdf/pdf_to_word, browser.pagination checkpoint) through validate_path_with_env_config(). It did not cover the data.* and file.* write families, which still write a client-controlled path with no confinement.Reachability (hop-by-hop, guards resolved)Client invokes a module via the recipe engine / MCP execute_module (src/core/mcp_handler.py, mcp_server.py) — the same surface as GHSA-2956 / CVE-2026-55786.data.csv.write reads file_path = params.get('file_path') and data (both client-controlled). Its only path check is if '..' in file_path: raise — a denylist that does not block absolute paths.It calls os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(file_path), exist_ok=True) then open(file_path, 'w') and writes data. No call to validate_path_with_env_config() — so FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement is never applied.data.json_to_csv (output_path), file.copy / file.move (shutil.copy2/shutil.move to destination) have no path check at all.An absolute path such as /home/<user>/.bashrc, /app/src/core/modules/.../<mod>.py, or a .flyto recipe file is written verbatim, outside the sandbox.Guard analysis: the GHSA-2956 enforcement is per-module (e.g. image/download.py:21 imports and calls validate_path_with_env_config). There is no central path enforcement in the runtime — runtime/languages.py's PathTraversalError guards plugin entry-point loading, not module output paths. So a module that omits the per-module call is entirely unconfined.Root causeThe remediation for GHSA-2956 confined writes by adding a per-module validate_path_with_env_config() call to an explicit list of modules, rather than enforcing confinement centrally. Any file-writing module absent from that list — the entire data.* and file.* families here — remains an arbitrary-write primitive. data.csv.write's '..'-substring check is a denylist that misses absolute paths.ImpactArbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content and path, escaping FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR. Overwriting a Python module under the install dir, a .flyto recipe, a shell rc, a crontab, or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys yields code execution / full host compromise — the same impact GHSA-2956 was rated Critical for.Executable PoC (benign sentinel, local only)FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR is set to the intended confinement; the module writes outside it while the GHSA-2956 guard rejects the same path.import os, sys, asyncioSBX = os.environ.setdefault('FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR', "/tmp/flyto_sbx"); os.makedirs(SBX, exist_ok=True)sys.path.insert(0, "<flyto-core>/src")OUT = "/tmp/flyto_PWNED_OUTSIDE.csv"           # absolute, outside the sandbox, no ".."from core.utils import validate_path_with_env_config, PathTraversalErrortry:    validate_path_with_env_config(OUT); print("[guard] UNEXPECTED allow")except PathTraversalError:    print("[guard] GHSA-2956 guard REJECTS out-of-sandbox path (as intended)")async def call(W, p): return await W(p, {}).execute()from core.modules.atomic.data.csv_write import csv_writefrom core.modules.atomic.data.json_to_csv import json_to_csvasyncio.run(call(csv_write,  {'file_path': OUT, 'data':[{'pwn':'SENTINEL_CSV'}]}))asyncio.run(call(json_to_csv,{'input_data':[{'pwn':'SENTINEL_JSON'}], 'output_path': OUT+'.json.csv'}))print("wrote outside sandbox:", os.path.exists(OUT),      "| inside sandbox?", os.path.realpath(OUT).startswith(os.path.realpath(SBX)))Observed output:[guard] GHSA-2956 guard validate_path_with_env_config() REJECTS out-of-sandbox path[data.csv.write]   wrote=True inside_sandbox=False[data.json_to_csv] wrote=True inside_sandbox=FalseBUG CONFIRMED (arbitrary write outside sandbox)  sample co

items.title: [django-docutils] django-docutils unsafe Docutils defaults allow local file disclosure, SSRF, and stored XSS
items.summary: Summarydjango-docutils before 0.30.0 rendered reStructuredText through Docutils without protected web-safe defaults. Public rendering paths, including publish_doctree, publish_html_from_source, publish_html_from_doctree, publish_parts_from_doctree, the {% rst %} template tag, the rst template filter, DocutilsTemplates, and DocutilsView, could process attacker-controlled RST with Docutils directives that read local files, fetch URL-backed content, or emit raw HTML.The issue is fixed in 0.30.0 by disabling Docutils file insertion, raw directives, local docutils.conf processing, and unsafe URI schemes by default, and by sanitizing doctrees before HTML is emitted.Applications are affected when they render attacker-controlled or lower-trust RST through django-docutils without their own safe Docutils configuration. Applications that only render trusted static RST are not affected unless that content can be influenced by an attacker.ImpactAn attacker who can influence RST rendered by a vulnerable django-docutils integration may be able to read files readable by the Django worker process, trigger server-side requests through URL-backed directives, or inject raw HTML/JavaScript into rendered output.Examples of affected application patterns include comments, wiki pages, blog bodies, profile or biography fields, CMS fields, uploaded RST documents, API-supplied RST, or overridden view content methods that return user-supplied RST.Potential impact includes disclosure of application configuration, environment files, credentials, source files, templates, mounted secrets, and logs readable by the process. UI escaping after rendering is not sufficient for file disclosure because the server-side read occurs before HTML reaches the client.Affected versionsAffected package: django-docutils on PyPIAffected versions: <= 0.29.0Patched versions: >= 0.30.0Technical detailsBefore 0.30.0, django-docutils handed RST content to Docutils without forcing these web-safe settings:{ "file_insertion_enabled": False, "raw_enabled": False, "_disable_config": True,}Docutils treats file insertion and raw content as legitimate features for trusted documents. In a web application that renders lower-trust RST, those defaults can expose server-side data or emit attacker-controlled HTML unless the application disables the features.The vulnerable behavior included:.. include:: reading local files.. include:: fetching URL-backed content server-side.. csv-table:: :file: reading local files.. csv-table:: :url: fetching URL-backed content server-side.. raw:: html emitting unescaped HTML.. raw:: html :file: reading and emitting file-backed raw contentlocal docutils.conf configuration re-enabling unsafe behaviorProof of conceptThis minimal harness uses the public {% rst %} template tag. On vulnerable versions, the include directive expands server-side and the raw directive emits unescaped HTML. On fixed versions, both directives are disabled under the default configuration.import djangofrom django.conf import settingssettings.configure( INSTALLED_APPS=["django_docutils"], TEMPLATES=[{ "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates", "DIRS": [], "APP_DIRS": False, "OPTIONS": {"libraries": {"dj": "django_docutils.templatetags.django_docutils"}}, }], # DJANGO_DOCUTILS_LIB_RST intentionally unset == default install.)django.setup()from django.template import enginesdj = engines["django"]def render_user_rst(rst: str) -> str: return dj.from_string("{% load dj %}{% rst content %}").render({"content": rst})print(render_user_rst(".. include:: /etc/passwd "))print(render_user_rst(".. raw:: html x "))Expected behavior on vulnerable releases such as 0.28.0 and 0.29.0:The include directive emits readable file contents.The raw directive emits x as HTML.Expected behavior on fixed releases such as 0.30.0 and later:The include directive is disabled.The raw directive is disabled.RemediationUpgrade to django-docutils 0.30.0 or later.For trusted static RST that intentionally depends on unsafe Docutils features, opt in explicitly:DJANGO_DOCUTILS_LIB_RST = { "allow_unsafe_docutils_settings": True, "docutils": { "raw_enabled": True, "file_insertion_enabled": True, "_disable_config": False, },}Do not enable unsafe Docutils settings for comments, profile text, CMS fields, uploaded files, API request data, or other lower-trust content.Note: django-docutils==0.30.0 has an undeclared runtime dependency on typing-extensions; install it alongside if your environment doesn't already provide it (tracked separately as a packaging fix).Relateddjango-docutils documentation: https://django-docutils.git-pull.comdjango-docutils 0.30.0:https://django-docutils.git-pull.com/history/#django-docutils-0-30-0-2026-06-07https://github.com/tony/django-docutils/blob/v0.30.0/CHANGES#django-docutils-0300-2026-06-07django-docutils security topic: https://django-docutils.git-pull.com/topi

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: ZIP package extraction follows in-root hardlinks and overwrites files outside the NLTK data root
items.summary: SummaryNLTK ships a security wrapper, nltk.pathsec.ZipFile, that is meant to confine archive extraction to trusted data roots and to block link-based escapes. When nltk.download() installs a package, the extraction write opens each member's target path without checking whether that path is a hardlink to a file located outside the data root. A local actor who can write inside a shared or predictable NLTK data root (for example ~/nltk_data, a group-writable /usr/share/nltk_data, or a shared container volume) can pre-plant an in-root hardlink at a member path that a soon-to-be-installed package will write. When the victim later runs the download, extraction truncates and overwrites the outside-root target through that hardlink. This is the same weakness class as the previously fixed downloader hardlink issue, but the fix did not reach the package-extraction write sink, so the latest published release remains exploitable through this path.Root CauseThe prior fix added an st_nlink > 1 refusal to the file-open helpers (nltk.pathsec.open / _hardened_open) and routed the downloader temporary-file write through that hardened opener, so a multiply-linked inode is refused on those paths. The extraction write sink was never given the same check. On published releases, nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract validates member names with validate_zip_archive and then delegates to the standard library extractor, whose plain open(targetpath, "wb") opens and truncates a pre-existing hardlink. The containment guard validate_zip_archive relies on Path.resolve() and name checks; resolve() follows symlinks (so a symlinked member is correctly refused) but a hardlink has a legitimate in-root name and in-root resolved path, so it passes. No code on the extraction path performs the st_nlink fstat that the sibling open helper performs.Affected component: nltk.pathsec (archive extraction), driven by nltk.downloaderReleased sink (<= 3.10.3): nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile.extract -> stdlib zipfile._extract_member -> open(targetpath, "wb")Containment guard that fails open for hardlinks: nltk/pathsec.py validate_zip_archive (name checks + Path.resolve())Development-branch sink: nltk/pathsec.py ZipFile._extract_member leaf reopen with O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC|O_NOFOLLOW (no st_nlink fstat)ImpactAn unprivileged local user who can create a file inside a data root that the victim's NLTK installation will extract into can cause the victim's process to truncate and overwrite a file outside that root. The attacker chooses which outside file is destroyed by selecting the hardlink target, so the integrity impact is complete for the chosen path (arbitrary outside-root file destruction). Where the victim resolves packages through an attacker-influenced mirror or index, the overwritten bytes are also attacker-chosen, which plausibly enables targeted file replacement and later code execution if the victim subsequently consumes the replaced file; that escalation is plausible rather than demonstrated here. Practical exploitation requires either that kernel hardlink protection (fs.protected_hardlinks) is disabled, or that the outside target is one the planting actor is permitted to hardlink (owned, writable, or group-shared), which is the same precondition carried by the previously accepted advisory for this weakness class.Proof of ConceptDependencies: a released nltk (3.10.3) installed from PyPI. The demonstration creates a data root, a victim file outside it, and a package archive whose member path is pre-planted as a hardlink to the victim file, then extracts through the security wrapper. It runs as a single user and succeeds even with fs.protected_hardlinks=1.Steps:Register a data root with nltk.data.path and create an extraction subtree inside it.Create a victim file outside the data root.Pre-plant an in-root hardlink at the member path the archive will write.Extract the archive through nltk.pathsec.ZipFile.extract.import os, sys, tempfile, zipfileimport nltkimport nltk.pathsec as pswork = tempfile.mkdtemp()data_root = os.path.join(work, "nltk_data")extract_root = os.path.join(data_root, "corpora")os.makedirs(os.path.join(extract_root, "pkgid"))nltk.data.path.insert(0, data_root)outside = os.path.join(work, "victim.txt")open(outside, "w").write("ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT")zippath = os.path.join(data_root, "pkg.zip")with zipfile.ZipFile(zippath, "w") as z:    z.writestr("pkgid/target", "PWNED-BY-EXTRACTION")member_abs = os.path.join(extract_root, "pkgid/target")os.link(outside, member_abs)  # pre-planted in-root hardlinkwith ps.ZipFile(zippath, "r") as z:    z.extract("pkgid/target", path=extract_root)print("victim now:", open(outside).read())victim now: PWNED-BY-EXTRACTIONThe equivalent test using a symlink instead of a hardlink is refused by validate_zip_archive with a Security Violation, isolating the missing guard to hardlinks on the extraction write.Attack ChainExposure: nltk.download() (and python -m nltk.downloader) is the shipped, default entry point; extraction of .zi

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: AllowlistUnpickler does not deny numpy submodule-local file-I/O sinks
items.summary: Summarynltk.picklesec.allowlisted_pickle_load keyed its denylist of dangerous globals by export name, so numpy's file-I/O callables that live in submodules and are not re-exported under __module__ == "numpy" were never matched. Under the broad allowed_modules=("numpy", "scipy", "sklearn") allowance that TransitionParser.parse(depgraphs, modelFile) granted for model files, a crafted protocol 4 pickle could name numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt (arbitrary file read, result returned to the caller of allowlisted_pickle_load) or numpy.lib.format.open_memmap (attacker-chosen file create), and the REDUCE opcode invoked them during the load.Affectednltk >= 3.10.0 and <= 3.10.3 (the allowlisting unpickler and the TransitionParser model path); numpy must be installed.ReproductionA pickle whose REDUCE names numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt with a target path, loaded through allowlisted_pickle_load(data, allowed_modules=("numpy",)), reads that file on v3.10.3; one naming numpy.lib.format.open_memmap with mode w+ creates a file. Both are refused on develop with UnpicklingError: global '...' is from a denied module. The maintainer transcript below shows the before and after runs.ImpactFile read and file create on the host that loads an untrusted model through NLTK's allowlisting unpickler. No code execution: this sits below the TransitionParser code-execution sibling GHSA-m396-3h67-vpfv, which is why the severity was reassessed to Medium (see the reply below).Editorial note (2026-10-10): the report body of this advisory had been overwritten with the text of GHSA-rv69-j573-cm47 (the nested gzip decompression bomb). The summary above was reconstructed by the maintainers from the title, the maintainer reply, the CVSS justification and PR #3757; the original reporter text is not recoverable from the record.Fix status (2026-09-28)Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).PR: #3778 "Bound decompression entry points in nltk (zip/gzip layers + pathsec.ZipFile + weka), CWE-409", merged 2026-08-25, merge commit 42d99b7a2 on develop. Fix commits: b6e0cedca (the nested gzip layer of a zip .gz member is bounded) and c6fe98211 (the decompression guards stream instead of buffering whole payloads).Probe: none. The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe (256 MiB of zeros gzipped into a STORED zip member declared at about 256 KiB, read through nltk.data.find().open().read()): refused with ValueError "Refusing to decompress suspected gzip bomb 'corpus/bomb.gz': it expands beyond nltk.data.MAX_UNZIP_RATIO=1000".Release: none yet; no release tag contains b6e0cedca.Maintainer reply (2026-09-28)Status: fixed on develop, unreleased.Fix verifiedThe numpy submodule file I/O sinks named in this report are denied on develop. This is fixed by PR #3757 ("Harden untrusted-model pickle allowlist (exact globals + numpy.lib denylist)"), merged into develop on 2026-08-20 as merge commit 628ebd2fa1b81d961edb6eff6b2eddd9d64588ba. The fix commit is a44a7af69bca87e92d9c4a701fcbbe4512e8d450 and the regression tests are in fb8da992b7b2ad082c69d2618ae2ac1c90c6b8b8.What the fix does. In nltk/picklesec.py the denylist no longer keys numpy sinks by export name; it now denies whole module prefixes. _DENIED_MODULE_PREFIXES gained numpy.lib, numpy.rec, numpy.core.records, numpy._core.records, numpy.ma.mrecords and numpy.compat, so numpy.lib.npyio, numpy.lib._npyio_impl and numpy.lib.format resolve inside a denied prefix and are refused under both request forms (the submodule module string and any top level re-export). In nltk/parse/transitionparser.py the model load no longer grants a broad allowed_modules=("numpy","scipy","sklearn"); it now uses allowed_modules=() plus an exact _MODEL_ALLOWED_GLOBALS list, and the model read is routed through pathsec.open.Before and after evidenceReproduced the report's own primitives with a protocol 4 REDUCE payload for numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt (arbitrary file read) and numpy.lib.format.open_memmap (arbitrary file create), loaded through allowlisted_pickle_load(allowed_modules=("numpy","scipy","sklearn")), and also driven through the real TransitionParser.parse product path. Judged by whether the sink actually touched a file, not by whether something raised. Interpreter: env -u PYTHONPATH /usr/local/bin/python3.13, CPython 3.13.7, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.18.1, sklearn 1.9.0.Before the fix, on release tag v3.10.3 (303f6e2ba), nltk 3.10.3:[READ ] recfromtxt sink reached = True   returned [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] (file was read)[WRITE] open_memmap sink reached = True   attacker chosen path created on disk[CTRL ] canonical numpy.load = refused: UnpicklingError (already denylisted in 3.10.3)[PROD ] TransitionParser.parse sink reached = True   model load passed the allowlist;        AttributeError after load: recarray has no attribute predict_proba (the read ran)VERDICT: SINK REACHED (vulnerable)After the fix, on develop (2fa3f48fe):[READ ] recfromtxt sink reached = False   refused: UnpicklingErro

items.title: [nltk] NLTK corpus-reader view methods bypass the scoped root sandbox via intermediate-directory symlinks
items.summary: affected: PyPI nltk >= 3.9.4 — CorpusReader.abspaths()/abspath() and the PlaintextCorpusReader / SyntaxCorpusReader view methodsdynamically reproduced: nltk 3.9.4 (8/9, scoped-escape checks), 3.10.3 (wheel, 9/9 checks) and master 6818767b9 (9/9 checks)Source references (file:line) are to commit 303f6e2b (release tag v3.10.3). Line numbers in the released nltk wheel match this tag exactly; master 6818767b9 contains the same code (pathsec.py renumbered by +44 lines from added hardening comments). In 3.9.4 the same logic exists at earlier line numbers (api.py:222-236 for open(), api.py:161-203 for abspath()/abspaths(), data.py:382-388 for the pointer open, pathsec.py:105-114 for the scoped branch); the affected code is identical.SummaryCorpusReader.open() (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py:235-257) is NLTK's hardened file-access entry point: after a lexical guard it calls validate_path(..., required_root=self._root) (api.py:246-249), and the scoped branch of pathsec.validate_path (nltk/pathsec.py:168-179) resolves symlinks and raises ValueError when the resolved target is not inside the corpus root. The view methods do not use this entry point: PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras (nltk/corpus/reader/plaintext.py:67-118) and SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words (api.py:473-519) build their streams from self.abspaths(fileids, ...) (api.py:174-217), which only does a lexical self._root.join(fileid) (nltk/data.py:452-469) and returns a FileSystemPathPointer. That pointer is opened via FileSystemPathPointer.open() → pathsec.open(raw_path, "rb") with required_root left at its default None (data.py:438-447, nltk/pathsec.py:752,783), so only the global allowed-roots check runs. The O_NOFOLLOW in _hardened_open (pathsec.py:676-731) protects only the final path component, so an intermediate-directory symlink inside the corpus root pointing at a sibling allowed root is followed by the kernel. A caller who places such a symlink (or loads an untrusted corpus containing one) can read any file that open() would refuse — files outside the corpus root yet inside the global NLTK data sandbox — via PlaintextCorpusReader.words([...]) / SyntaxCorpusReader.words([...]) (and the abspaths()-returned pointer), defeating the scoped escape protection that GHSA-p4rw-class fixes and test_required_root_blocks_symlink_escape were added for.DetailsRoot cause: two sibling file-access channels on the same CorpusReader disagree about the scoped sandbox.CorpusReader.open() (api.py:235-257) — the guarded channel:Layer 1 lexical guard (api.py:240-242) rejects absolute paths and ...Layer 2 scoped guard (api.py:246-249) calls pathsec.validate_path(path, context="CorpusReader", required_root=self._root).The required_root branch (pathsec.py:168-179) resolves the target with Path(raw).resolve() and raises ValueError when target.is_relative_to(scoped_root) is false.The view-method channel — abspaths() → FileSystemPathPointer → pathsec.open(required_root=None):CorpusReader.abspath() (api.py:174-183) and abspaths() (api.py:185-217) return self._root.join(f) with no validate_path call.FileSystemPathPointer.join() (data.py:452-469) only normalizes lexically (normpath + root-prefix startswith); it never calls os.path.realpath/Path.resolve, so the intermediate symlink is preserved verbatim.FileSystemPathPointer.open() (data.py:438-447) calls _secure_open(self._path, "rb") (aliased from pathsec.open) with no required_root, so pathsec.open (pathsec.py:752) uses its default required_root=None and validate_path (pathsec.py:783) runs only the global allowed-roots check (pathsec.py:181-207).Under ENFORCE=True + POSIX, _hardened_open (pathsec.py:676-731) opens with O_NOFOLLOW (pathsec.py:705) — but that flag only refuses a symlink in the final component; an intermediate directory symlink (corpus/sub -> <other allowed root>) is followed by the kernel. The post-open fd realpath re-validation (pathsec.py:728-731) again uses required_root=None, and since the target is inside an allowed root it passes.The view methods hand the unguarded pointers straight to the stream views:PlaintextCorpusReader.words/sents/paras (plaintext.py:67-118, abspaths at 76/96/116) and chapters (plaintext.py:230).SyntaxCorpusReader.parsed_sents/tagged_sents/sents/tagged_words/words (api.py:473-519, abspaths at 478/489/498/509/517).StreamBackedCorpusView._open() (nltk/corpus/reader/util.py:203-216) calls self._fileid.open(self._encoding) on the PathPointer (util.py:210), landing in the required_root=None path above.Net effect (observed): the identical fileid "sub/secret.txt" is rejected by reader.open() with ValueError: Security Violation [CorpusReader]: Path ... escapes root ... but successfully read by reader.words(["sub/secret.txt"]), returning the out-of-root file's content.The abspaths()/view-method bypass contradicts the contract stated in open()'s docstring (api.py:238, "Security patched: prevents path traversal and scoped escapes") and the class-level promise

items.title: [nltk] NLTK incomplete fix: additional JVM/JAR sandbox bypass through unvalidated launcher tokens in java() command arguments
items.summary: SummaryNLTK 3.10.3 contains security hardening intended to close JVM argument-injection and untrusted JAR/classpath execution paths in nltk.internals.java(), including the issue published as GHSA-m4rf-3fr8-xwx3.The patched options channel correctly rejects Java argument-file references such as @/path/to/args and launcher modes such as -jar. However, an additional argument channel remains: the caller-provided cmd sequence is appended to the Java command after the validated option and classpath channels, without enforcing that its first item is a Java main-class name.I am reporting this as an additional post-fix bypass / incomplete-fix path affecting the 3.10.3 remediation, rather than as an unrelated vulnerability family.As a result, the same launcher token that is rejected through options can be supplied as the first cmd item. I confirmed two reachable forms against the official nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whl:direct use of the public nltk.internals.java() helper with cmd=["-jar", ...]; andthe higher-level StanfordSegmenter, whose public java_class constructor argument becomes the first cmd item and accepts an @argfile launcher token.Both paths execute an external researcher-controlled JAR without setting NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_JARS, NLTK_ALLOW_UNSAFE_CLASSPATH, or using trusted_raw_options. The original explicit outside-classpath route is blocked in 3.10.3, while the alternate command channel executes the JAR 3/3 times.Affected artifactPackage: nltkConfirmed affected version: 3.10.3Wheel: nltk-3.10.3-py3-none-any.whlSHA-256: ff9598a8e20518ee0d557745890cc4435b9578489e2dcbc69c4f81fa060caf7cBaseline artifact:Version: 3.10.2Wheel: nltk-3.10.2-py3-none-any.whlSHA-256: 2c7ccacb765c5e26b0cb60fb1b57080af522c6924d12a714a243305ba3637412Relationship to the 3.10.3 security fixesThe existing 3.10.3 hardening validates the dedicated per-call options list before it reaches subprocess.Popen. In particular, the exact @argfile token used in this report is rejected through options with a ValueError that references CVE-2026-12841 and CWE-88.The command is subsequently assembled in this order:final_cmd.extend(validated_options)if classpath_arg is not None:    final_cmd.extend(["-cp", classpath_arg])final_cmd.extend(cmd_list)cmd_list is copied from the public cmd argument but its first token is not checked to ensure that it is an ordinary Java main class. Java therefore interprets leading -jar, @argfile, module-mode, or classpath-mode tokens as launcher control arguments rather than application arguments.This is an alternate argument channel around the same JVM argument/JAR execution boundary protected by the 3.10.3 changes.Confirmed API pathsDirect public helpernltk.internals.java(    ["-jar", "/outside/trusted/roots/controlled.jar"],    classpath=None,    stdout="pipe",    stderr="pipe",)The external JAR executed in all three subject runs.Higher-level StanfordSegmenter pathStanfordSegmenter exposes a public java_class constructor argument, stores it, and later places it at the beginning of the cmd sequence passed to nltk.internals.java().A controlled argument file containing a -jar launcher invocation was supplied as:StanfordSegmenter(    path_to_jar=trusted_segmenter_jar,    java_class="@/path/to/controlled-launcher.args",    path_to_model="dummy-model",    java_options=[],)The trusted segmenter JAR passed the wrapper's checksum and classpath checks. The @argfile then switched the Java launcher to the external JAR, which executed in all three runs.The deprecated wrapper subsequently raised an unrelated post-launch AttributeError while processing its output. The external marker had already been written by the child JVM before that exception.Proof matrixR1  NLTK 3.10.2 + explicit external classpath    -> controlled Java bytecode executedR2  NLTK 3.10.3 + same explicit external classpath    -> UntrustedJarError; no markerR3A NLTK 3.10.3 + direct cmd=["-jar", external_jar]    -> controlled external JAR executed, 3/3R3B NLTK 3.10.3 + StanfordSegmenter(java_class="@argfile")    -> controlled external JAR executed, 3/3R4  NLTK 3.10.3 + ordinary main class in trusted classpath    -> legitimate execution preservedA direct channel comparison also confirmed:options=["@argfile"]       -> BLOCKEDcmd/java_class="@argfile"  -> EXTERNAL JAR EXECUTEDMachine-readable proof results and a portable reproducer are attached.PreconditionsPractical exploitability depends on an embedding application exposing attacker influence over one of these public argument paths:the leading item of nltk.internals.java(cmd=...); orStanfordSegmenter(java_class=...) or an equivalent wrapper-controlled command token.The attacker must also be able to reference an argument file or JAR readable by the NLTK process. The Java child process executes with the privileges of that process.This is not a claim that importing NLTK alone is remotely exploitable. items.title: [nltk] NLTK: XMLCorpusView comment and CDATA parsing permits quadratic CPU denial of service
items.summary: affected: PyPI nltk >= 3.6 — nltk.corpus.reader.xmldocs.XMLCorpusView streaming read (and the nps_chat / framenet readers built on it)dynamically reproduced: 3.6 (6/6 checks), 3.9.2 (6/6), 3.10.3 (6/6) and develop 6818767b9 (6/6)Source references (nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py:NNN) are to commit 6818767b99c24659107eb2be9bccd32a3d4bf045 (develop, v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9). The released v3.10.3 wheel's xmldocs.py is byte-identical to that commit, so the same line numbers apply to the released wheel.SummaryAn attacker who can make a victim read a well-formed XML corpus file whose body contains one large comment or CDATA section can pin a CPU core for a time quadratic in the file size, because XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment (nltk/corpus/reader/xmldocs.py) re-runs a linear whole-buffer validation after every 1 KiB block while the comment/CDATA terminator is still ahead. XMLCorpusView is NLTK's documented streaming API for XML corpora and is instantiated directly by the NPSChatCorpusReader and FramenetCorpusReader readers; the module header (xmldocs.py:16-20) explicitly handles untrusted corpus XML. The in_tag guard added to this function for GHSA-vp2x covers only a single oversized <...> tag and leaves the CDATA/comment path quadratic in the current release.DetailsRoot cause: _read_xml_fragment (xmldocs.py:273-338) accumulates the file into one fragment string in _BLOCK_SIZE (1024) character chunks (xmldocs.py:123, 298-299). After every block that is not yet a well-formed prefix, the fragment is re-validated against _VALID_XML_RE. Two whole-buffer operations dominate:# xmldocs.py:308if not in_tag and self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment):      # whole-buffer match (O(len))    return fragment# xmldocs.py:312if re.search("[<>]", fragment).group(0) == ">":            # O(1) for this input class:    ...                                                     # the document starts with '<'# xmldocs.py:329if self._VALID_XML_RE.match(fragment[:last_open_bracket]): # whole-buffer prefix match (O(len))    ...For this input class the re.search probe at xmldocs.py:312 is O(1): the fragment always starts with < (e.g. <root>…), so the first </> character is at offset 0 and it never contributes cost. The quadratic cost comes entirely from the two whole-buffer regex matches at xmldocs.py:308 and xmldocs.py:329 (the latter scans the buffer up to the most recent <, which for this input sits near the end of the buffer)._VALID_XML_RE (xmldocs.py:238-249) is a linear regex (its tempered-dot comment/CDATA bodies (?:(?!-->).)* / (?:(?!\]\]>).)* scan left-to-right in O(length) — confirmed by the embedded script's single-match check), but for a fragment whose terminator is far ahead the match itself fails after scanning the whole buffer. With an unclosed-across-blocks CDATA or comment, every one of the n/1024 blocks pays O(current buffer length) on lines 308 and 329, for a total of ~O(n²) character operations.The in_tag guard added for GHSA-vp2x (xmldocs.py:283-305) tracks only bare </> characters: it is True inside an unclosed <...> tag and, in that state, skips only the line-308 match. It never represents "the fragment sits inside an unclosed CDATA or comment" — XML allows arbitrary </> inside those constructs — so both the line-308 match and the line-329 backtrack match still fire on every block for a CDATA/comment fragment. The comment block at xmldocs.py:283-289 even documents the intended linearity contract ("re-running it on every 1 KiB block otherwise makes a single oversized tag O(n^2) (CWE-407)"); the guard implements it for the tag branch only.The single-match cost is linear, not super-linear: the embedded script measures _VALID_XML_RE.match() on 512 KiB → 1 MiB → 2 MiB unclosed-CDATA buffers and gets ≈ 0.074 s → 0.142 s → 0.280 s (≈ 1:1.9:3.8, i.e. linear), asserting the 4× ratio stays well below the quadratic bound. The quadratic total therefore comes from re-running those linear matches per block — the exact CWE-407 pattern the in-tag guard was introduced to eliminate.Version nuance (all dynamically verified):3.10.3 / develop (guard present): the pinned regex validates CDATA correctly, so both the comment and the CDATA attack documents read successfully and return; both scale super-linearly (t(4n)/t(n) ≈ 13-16; linear would be ≈ 4). The oversized single-tag control reads linearly (ratio ≈ 4.0), proving the quadratic cost is specific to the unguarded CDATA/comment path.3.6 / 3.9.2 (pre-guard): these releases use a lazy _VALID_XML_RE whose CDATA alternative <![CDATA[.*?]]> never matches (the [CDATA[.*?] substring is parsed as a character class), so a CDATA document is rejected with ValueError: Unexpected end of file: tag not closed after the quadratic scan — a separate functional defect. The comment variant is a clean well-formed document on these releases and is likewise quadratic (t(4n)/t(n) ≈ 14-16); the oversized-tag control also reads quadratically there (ratio ≈ 16), i.e. the whole unclosed-construct class GHSA-vp2x addressed

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Downloader cyclic collection indices cause an infinite closure walk
items.summary: affected: PyPI nltk >= 3.6.7 — nltk.downloader index parsing (Downloader._update_index)dynamically reproduced: nltk 3.6.7 (4/4 checks), 3.9.2 (4/4), 3.10.3 (4/4), and develop 6818767b9 (4/4)Source references (nltk/downloader.py:NNN) are to commit 6818767b9 (develop, v3.10.3-15-g6818767b9). The v3.10.3 tag and the released 3.10.3 wheel carry the identical code at the identical line numbers (the vulnerable closure BFS sits at downloader.py:1300-1310). Dynamically verified wheels additionally show the same defect at downloader.py:972 (3.9.2) and downloader.py:987 (3.6.7).SummaryDownloader._update_index (nltk/downloader.py:1253-1313) is the mandatory first step of every downloader operation (download(), info(), packages(), collections(), list(), status()). After replacing each <item ref="…"> string with the actual Collection/Package object (downloader.py:1285-1290), it computes each collection's recursive package closure with a breadth-first walk that has no visited set and no depth cap:# nltk/downloader.py:1300-1310for collection in self._collections.values():    packages = {}    queue = [collection]    for child in queue:        if isinstance(child, Collection):            queue.extend(child.children)        elif isinstance(child, Package):            packages[child.id] = child    collection.packages = packages.values()A self-referencing or mutually-referencing index — e.g. <collection id="a"><item ref="a"/></collection> — turns a.children into an object-level cycle, and the for child in queue: queue.extend(child.children) loop appends to the very list it is iterating, so the queue grows forever. The function never returns: CPU spins at 100% and memory grows without bound until the process is killed or the host runs out of memory. The identical finite input (one collection containing one package) completes in ~0.2 s on the control index, so the input is perfectly ordinary in size — only its self-reference is abnormal, and nothing validates it.DetailsRoot cause is the combination of three unguarded steps:Collection.fromxml (nltk/downloader.py:362-369) stores each <item ref="…"> attribute verbatim as a string. It never checks whether a ref targets the collection's own id, or participates in a reference cycle._update_index (nltk/downloader.py:1285-1290) replaces those ref strings with the live objects from self._collections / self._packages. A self- or mutual-reference therefore becomes an object-level cycle in children.The closure walk (nltk/downloader.py:1300-1310) iterates for child in queue while doing queue.extend(child.children) inside the loop. Python's list iterator consumes elements appended during iteration, so with a cycle the iterator and the queue length advance in lockstep forever. There is no visited set, no node-count cap, and no cycle detection.The input is the data-server index that the downloader is designed to fetch and trust: _update_index pulls it with safe_parse(urlopen(self._url)) (nltk/downloader.py:1269-1271) and parses <collections>/<collection> elements with no structural validation. The index URL is a user-configurable product feature (server_index_url constructor argument, CLI -u / --url at downloader.py:3052-3058 — the option's dest is server_index_url — plus NLTK_DOWNLOAD_URL and the Shell/GUI "Set Server URL"), so an operator who uses a third-party mirror, or whose configured mirror is compromised, delivers the malicious index into exactly this code path on the next download or query.PoCThe self-checking reproduction script embedded below runs the attack against a file://-hosted index (no network server needed; the hardened nltk.pathsec.urlopen accepts local file:// URLs) and a matching acyclic control index, in separate child processes under an address-space cap (RLIMIT_AS). That is the key to demonstrating the vulnerability safely and precisely: the control process completes under the cap, while the attack process — the same function, the same caller, the same finite 2-entry index — cannot finish and is aborted by MemoryError at queue.extend(child.children), proving both the hang (the function never returns) and the unbounded memory growth (a 2-entry index growing until the address-space cap is exhausted). Without the cap the loop simply runs forever.Scope note: dynamically verified on the released 3.6.7, 3.9.2, and 3.10.3 wheels and on develop 6818767b9. 3.6.0–3.6.6 share the identical BFS code path (verified statically at the tag) but were not run; the downloader tool predates 3.6 and earlier releases were not assessed.Environment for the recorded run: CPython 3.10.12 on Linux; the script defaults to a 512 MiB address-space cap per child and a 60 s hard timeout. All four version runs pass 4/4 checks.Live transcript (recorded run on the nltk 3.10.3 wheel; the 3.6.7, 3.9.2, and develop 6818767b9 runs produce the same 4/4 result, differing only in the downloader.py line number in the traceback — 987, 972, and 1305 respectively — and the elapsed time):[PASS] precondition: cyclic

[nltk] Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK): Uncontrolled recursion (crash DoS) in DependencyGraph.tree()/triples()
items.summary: SummaryDependencyGraph.tree()/triples() walk the parsed dependency structure using plain, unbounded Python recursion — one stack frame per edge in the graph — and never use the class's own cycle detector. A crafted dependency-parse file with a few thousand chained tokens (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence) crashes the process with an unhandled RecursionError the moment .tree() or .triples() is called — which is NLTK's own documented usage pattern immediately after loading such a file.DetailsDependencyGraph._tree() (lines 393-406), .tree() (408-417), and .triples() (419-432) in nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py rebuild/walk the graph with Tree(word, [self._tree(dep) for dep in deps]) and yield from self.triples(node=dep) — ordinary recursive calls, one per edge, with no depth check. contains_cycle() is defined on the class (line 447) but is never invoked by any of these three methods.This is exactly the CWE-674 pattern the project has already identified and fixed elsewhere: nltk/tree/tree.py adds MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 500 with a comment stating that an arbitrarily deep tree would make every traversal raise RecursionError, and nltk/test/unit/test_recursion_dos.py locks in the identical fix for FeatStructReader, LogicParser, and ResolutionProver. But DependencyGraph builds its Tree objects programmatically (Tree(word, [...])), which bypasses MAX_TREE_DEPTH entirely — that guard only fires inside Tree.fromstring()'s bracket-string parser, never in Tree.__init__. DependencyGraph's own recursive walk has no depth limit of its own.Any Malt-TAB/CoNLL(3/4/7/10)-format text — read via DependencyCorpusReader (nltk/corpus/reader/dependency.py, lines 62-69, backing the public, documented nltk.corpus.dependency_treebank and nltk.corpus.conll2007 corpora) or via the public classmethod DependencyGraph.load(filename) (~line 213) / DependencyGraph(text) directly — that chains more tokens than Python's default recursion limit (1000) via consecutive head references crashes with an unhandled RecursionError the moment .tree()/.triples() is called. Calling .tree() immediately after parsed_sents() is not a contrived edge case — it is NLTK's own documented usage pattern (nltk/test/corpus.doctest: print(conll2007.parsed_sents('esp.train')[0].tree()); nltk/test/dependency.doctest: dg.tree().pprint()).Related observation: contains_cycle() itself has a separate bug that means it wouldn't help even if it were called on this path — it iterates node["deps"] as if it were a flat list of neighbor addresses, but _parse()/add_arc() actually store deps as {relation_label: [addresses]}; iterating that dict yields relation-label strings, which then fail the dep not in self.nodes check and get silently skipped. So contains_cycle() returns False (a false negative) on real parsed/add_arc()-built graphs even when a genuine cycle exists — it only works on the flat-list shape used in its own docstring example. This reinforces that there is no working recursion/cycle safety net on this code path today.PoCA tiny (few KB) 3-column Malt-TAB file: one root line w1 ROOT 0 followed by ~2000-3000 lines wi X i-1, each chaining a token to the previous one (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence/coordination structure). Verified directly against current source:Constructing a DependencyGraph from a 3000-token linear chain and calling .tree() → RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. Confirmed.Same graph, .triples() fully consumed → RecursionError. Confirmed.Full realistic path: wrote the 3000-token chain to a temp file, read it back through an actual DependencyCorpusReader (the exact class backing dependency_treebank/conll2007) via parsed_sents(), then called .tree() on the result → RecursionError, end-to-end through the real public API.(One honest correction to an earlier draft of this finding: a "two lines whose head columns reference each other" file-based cycle does not actually reach this crash the way it might seem — in the single-head-per-token Malt-TAB/CoNLL format, a genuine mutual-reference pair can't simultaneously be reachable from the graph's root and form a back-edge, so it either leaves self.root = None, or the pair becomes a disconnected island that's silently walked past without crashing. The long-chain vector above is the one that's fully, independently confirmed; a cycle built via direct add_arc() graph manipulation does also crash, but that's a narrower trigger than a parsed file.)ImpactAn unauthenticated party who can get a crafted CoNLL/Malt-TAB dependency file processed by a downstream application — a treebank upload, a shared-task submission portal, a user-editable corpus directory, or any code calling DependencyGraph.load()/DependencyGraph() on user-supplied text — crashes that request/worker/script with no further interaction needed. 100% reliable, trivial to construct.Suggested fix: apply the same MAX_TREE_DEPTH-style depth guard used elsewhere in the codebase to _tree()/tree()/triples(), and fix contains_cycle()'s dict-vs

items.title: [nltk] Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK): Uncontrolled recursion (crash DoS) in Synset.tree()/acyclic_tree() via WordNet relation traversal
items.summary: SummaryThe recursive traversal engines behind WordNetCorpusReader's Synset.tree() and Synset.acyclic_tree() have no maximum call-depth safeguard and default to unlimited depth. They guard against literal cycles, but not against a long, genuinely acyclic relation chain — which exhausts the Python call stack the same way as the sibling DependencyGraph finding I reported separately. Real-world exploitability requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource rather than NLTK's bundled default corpus — flagging that narrower scope honestly up front since it affects severity, not validity.Detailsnltk/util.py's acyclic_depth_first() (lines 471-541) and acyclic_branches_depth_first() (lines 544-625) recurse once per graph edge, default to depth=-1 ("unlimited"), and guard against re-visiting the same node via an explicit traversed set (hence "acyclic") — but that set only prevents literal cycles, it never bounds how many distinct nodes a single call chain may pass through before returning.Synset.tree(rel, depth=-1) (nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py, ~line 664) calls the recursive acyclic_branches_depth_first. There is also a third, easy-to-miss method: Synset.acyclic_tree(), a vestigial class-attribute alias for acyclic_depth_first — also genuinely recursive and vulnerable.Important correction to an earlier draft of this finding: Synset.closure(rel, depth=-1) (~line 609) does not share this bug — it actually calls acyclic_breadth_first(), a completely different, iterative queue/deque-based function with no recursion at all. I verified this directly: feeding both acyclic_breadth_first and the real Synset.closure() a 20,000-node genuinely-acyclic chain produces zero crash, while acyclic_depth_first/acyclic_branches_depth_first/Synset.tree()/Synset.acyclic_tree() crash reliably at ~1000-1500 nodes on the identical data. Only .tree() and .acyclic_tree() are affected — not .closure().This is the same CWE-674 pattern already hardened elsewhere in the codebase (MAX_TREE_DEPTH in tree/tree.py, MAX_DEPTH in featstruct.py, MAX_PARSE_DEPTH in logic.py, MAX_TABLEAU_DEPTH in tableau.py, MAX_DECODE_DEPTH in jsontags.py, added by a commit whose message explicitly enumerates the sinks it covers) — but that hardening pass never reached nltk/util.py or wordnet.py.Honest scope-limiting fact: I exhaustively measured the maximum possible traversal depth across the entire official, bundled WordNet 3.0 corpus (what the overwhelming majority of real deployments use) for every relation NLTK exposes to tree(): hypernyms/hyponyms max depth = 18 (across all 74,374 noun synsets); also_sees (a relation whose graph isn't curated to stay as shallow as the taxonomy) max eccentricity = 41, largest connected component = 824 nodes; similar_tos max eccentricity = 1; entailments/causes/verb_groups/member_holonyms/member_meronyms/attributes all ≤ 11. Every one of these is roughly 25-60x below the ~1000-node crash threshold — there is no word or relation an attacker could pick against the standard bundled corpus that reaches anywhere near a crash. nltk.app.wordnet_app, NLTK's own bundled reference consumer, only ever calls .tree() with the safe hypernym relation.Real-world exploitability therefore strictly requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource — a legitimate, documented, WordNetCorpusReader-supported usage, but a comparatively uncommon one — and then call .tree()/.acyclic_tree() (not .closure()) with the default unbounded depth.PoCGenerated a syntactically valid, minimal, real Princeton-WordNet-DB-format lexical database (data.noun/index.noun/lexnames/etc., with correct byte-offset-indexed synset records) encoding a 1500-node strictly-linear (genuinely acyclic) hypernym chain. Loaded it via the real, unmodified WordNetCorpusReader(root, None), obtained a real Synset, and called the real, documented, public synset.tree(lambda s: s.hypernyms()) — crashed with an uncaught RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded, as did synset.acyclic_tree(...). synset.closure(...) on the identical data returned cleanly (1499 nodes, no crash), confirming the closure()/tree() distinction above.ImpactAn application that loads a custom WordNet-format lexical resource (e.g. a domain-specific or community-contributed WordNet, which WordNetCorpusReader is explicitly designed to support) and calls .tree()/.acyclic_tree() with an attacker-influenced or simply not-officially-curated relation/resource can be crashed via an unhandled RecursionError from a single long-but-acyclic relation chain. Narrower reach than a bundled-default-corpus bug, but a real, working, unpatched gap in the same CWE-674 family the project actively hardens elsewhere.Suggested fix: apply the same MAX_TREE_DEPTH-style depth guard to acyclic_depth_first()/acyclic_branches_depth_first() (or reuse the existing Tree constant/pattern directly).Fix status (2026-09-28)Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in CCG lexicon parser causes denial of service via deeply nested category input
items.summary: Root CauseThe CCG lexicon parser recurses on nested parenthesised categories without any depthbound. matchBrackets (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:154) calls itself once per nested (, andaugParseCategory (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:228,242) recurses once per bracketedsub-category. Neither function tracks recursion depth nor checkssys.getrecursionlimit(), and the public entry point fromstring(nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:252, also re-exported via nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring) applies nolength or nesting cap before handing the text to the parser.ImpactAn application that parses an untrusted lexicon string aborts with an unhandledRecursionError, terminating the affected parse operation or request worker(denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is pure Python, so CPython raises a catchableRecursionError rather than crashing the process; there is no memory-corruption orcode-execution primitive. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. Plausibly, aservice that does not wrap the parse in a handler will surface the error to the caller anddrop the in-flight request.Attack ChainThe application calls nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str) with attacker-suppliedtext such as ":- S\nw => " + "(" * 2000 + "S" + ")" * 2000 + "\n".fromstring splits the input into lines; LEX_RE/RHS_RE(nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:275-276) match and route the parenthesised category intoaugParseCategory (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:277) with no depth or length guard.Because the category starts with (, nextCategory dispatches to matchBrackets,which recurses once per nested (; augParseCategory recurses once per bracketedsub-category. Each nesting level consumes call-stack frames.Once the depth exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled RecursionErrorpropagates out of the public API and aborts the parse.Bypass EvidenceRunning the dependency-free matchBrackets body verbatim from the shipped source at thedefault recursion limit (1000): a well-formed balanced input at depth 5 and 500 parsescleanly, while depth 2000 and 5000 raise an unhandled RecursionError. Because shallow,balanced input parses without error, the failure is depth-driven rather than a genericparse error. The crash triggers near ~1000 nesting levels at the default limit, so thepayload need not be extreme. A repository-wide search confirms no depth/recursion guardexists anywhere under nltk/ccg/ (the only recent change to this file routed regexesthrough nltk.redos and added no recursion bound).Suggested FixAdd a recursion-depth choke point on the lexicon-parsing path — for example a depthcounter that raises a bounded ValueError past a configurable maximum, mirroring theexisting guards on FeatStructReader (nltk/featstruct.py), Tree.fromstring(MAX_TREE_DEPTH, nltk/tree/tree.py), and LogicParser (MAX_PARSE_DEPTH,nltk/sem/logic.py).Reported by pi (GitHub: @manus-pi).Fix status (2026-09-28)Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).PR: #3885 "Bound recursion depth in parsers and traversal helpers" (ekaf), merged 2026-09-11, merge commit e521ecafc on develop.Fix commit: 30e93eb7b (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py: matchBrackets and the category parser stop at MAX_PARSE_DEPTH=500 with ValueError).Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_3h95_x772_4765.py (added in 2a6704952 on that PR); verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (bounded (ValueError)).Release: none yet; no release tag contains e521ecafc.Referenceshttps://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-3h95-x772-4765https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129224https://github.com/nltk/nltk/pull/3885https://github.com/nltk/nltk/commit/30e93eb7b69021293e019042fe0cedb99c95b054https://github.com/nltk/nltk/releases/tag/v3.10.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3h95-x772-4765

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in DependencyGraph traversal causes denial of service via deep dependency chains
items.summary: Root CauseThe dependency-graph traversal helpers recurse over dependency links without any depthbound or visited set. DependencyGraph._tree (nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:404)recurses once per dependency link, triples (nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:432) is arecursive generator, and get_cycle_path (nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:520) recursesover dependencies. The recursion is purePython, so the result is a catchable RecursionError, not memory corruption or codeexecution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. get_cycle_path additionallylacks a visited set and will not terminate on a genuine cycle.Attack ChainThe application constructs DependencyGraph(conll_str) from attacker-supplied textwhere token k's head is token k+1, forming a linear dependency chain of length N.Graph construction (_parse) is iterative and completes without error.The application calls the public DependencyGraph.tree()(nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:408), which invokes _tree(root)._tree recurses once per chain link with no depth guard and no visited set, consumingone stack frame per link (the list comprehension costs roughly two frames per level).Once the chain length exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandledRecursionError propagates out of the public API. triples() fails the same way.Bypass EvidenceAgainst the shipped source at the default recursion limit, a chain of length 5 walkscleanly through tree(), while a chain of length 5000 raises an unhandledRecursionError; triples() fails identically. The minimal trigger is roughly N=500tokens at the default recursion limit — a modest, realistic parse. Because the graphbuilds iteratively in both cases, the fault is isolated to the recursive traversal ratherthan to parsing. items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in Tree.fromlist causes denial of service via deeply nested list input
